cards.text: Meet Manasseh, king of Judah. He takes the throne in Jerusalem at twelve years old and reigns FIFTY-FIVE years. Twelve! I know grown adults who can't pick a ringtone, and this young man is running a kingdom.

cards.question: Manasseh does evil in the sight of the LORD. Whose abominations does he follow?

answers.text: The nations the LORD drove out

cards.text: Here's what that looks like. His father Hezekiah had destroyed the high places.

cards.question: Manasseh keeps the high places his father destroyed torn down.

cards.text: Manasseh rebuilds them, and he raises up altars for Baal too. That's like canceling every subscription you've got, and somebody signs you right back up for all of them PLUS a few new ones.

cards.question: Manasseh also makes an Asherah pole, just as King ___ of Israel had done.

cards.text: He worships and serves all the host of heaven. Now, about His own house, the LORD had said, "In Jerusalem I will put My Name."

cards.question: Where does Manasseh build altars to all the host of heaven?

answers.text: In the house of the LORD

cards.text: In both courtyards of the LORD's house. Then comes the darkest line in this whole passage: Manasseh sacrifices his own son in the fire.

cards.question: Manasseh practices sorcery and divination, and he consults ___ and spiritists.

cards.text: He does great evil in the sight of the LORD, provoking Him to anger. Then he takes the carved Asherah pole he made and sets it up in the temple itself.
This is the temple the LORD spoke about to King David and his son Solomon: "In this temple and in Jerusalem, which I have chosen out of all the tribes of Israel, I will establish My Name forever."

cards.question: God also promised He'd never again make Israel wander from the land He gave their fathers. What was the condition?

answers.text: They had to do all He commanded
They had to defeat their enemies
They had to build Him more altars

cards.question: The people of Judah refuse to follow Manasseh into evil.
Manasseh leads the people astray. How does their evil compare to the nations the LORD destroyed before Israel?

cards.text: Greater. Let that sink in, friend. The people God brought into this land are now doing greater evil than the nations He destroyed before them.
The LORD doesn't stay quiet. He speaks through His servants the prophets: Manasseh has acted more wickedly than the Amorites who came before him, and with his idols he has caused Judah to sin.

cards.question: The LORD says He is bringing peace and security to Jerusalem and Judah.

cards.text: He's bringing calamity, so big the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it. Not one little group chat ping, friend, but every phone in town buzzing at the SAME time.

God says He'll stretch over Jerusalem the measuring line used against Samaria and the plumb line used against the house of Ahab. Then He gives a picture I know from my own kitchen: He'll wipe out Jerusalem as one wipes out a bowl.

cards.question: God says He'll wipe out Jerusalem like a bowl. After the wiping, what happens to the bowl?

cards.text: Wiped clean and flipped over, not a crumb left. I've wiped out more mixing bowls than I can count, and not ONE of them ever sounded this serious.

cards.question: What does God say He will do with the remnant of His inheritance?

cards.text: They'll become plunder and spoil to all their enemies. And God gives the reason in His own words.

cards.question: God says they have provoked Him to anger from the day their fathers came out of ___ until this day.

cards.text: On top of all that, Manasseh sheds so much innocent blood that he fills Jerusalem from end to end. The rest of what he did is written in the Book of the Chronicles of the Kings of Judah.

cards.question: After his long reign, Manasseh rests with his fathers. Where is he buried?

cards.text: The garden of Uzza, to be exact. His son Amon takes the throne at twenty-two and reigns in Jerusalem two years, which is about as long as a phone contract.

cards.question: Amon turns away from his father's evil and does what is right in the sight of the LORD.
Amon walks in all the ways of his father, and he serves and worships the ___ his father had served.

cards.text: He abandons the LORD, the God of his fathers, and doesn't walk in the way of the LORD. Then a plot forms against the king.

cards.question: Who conspires against King Amon and kills him in his palace?
The people of the land side with the servants who killed King Amon.

cards.text: The people of the land kill all those who conspired against Amon and make his son Josiah king in his place. Amon is buried in his tomb in the garden of Uzza, and young Josiah takes the throne.

findings.problem: The opening card has 4 sentences: "Meet Manasseh, king of Judah." / "He takes the throne..." / "Twelve!" / "I know grown adults..."

rule.text: The opening card can be up to 3 sentences. It says who is speaking, to whom, and what is going on.

findings.problem: The ringtone joke laughs at other people ("grown adults who can't pick a ringtone") instead of at Papa Dorin himself. It also leans toward a joke about people's competence.

rule.text: Humble. When a joke needs someone to laugh at, it's himself.

findings.problem: The right answer "The nations the LORD drove out" is twice as long as the wrong answers and is the only one in Bible-sounding wording, so it stands out from "His father Hezekiah" and "The prophet Isaiah".

rule.text: Don't let the right answer stand out. All the answers should sound alike. None should sound more like the Bible, or more modern, than the others.

findings.problem: This is a recap card. It repeats the answer to card 15 ("Greater... doing greater evil than the nations He destroyed before them") and tells nothing new from the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: This is a recap card. It repeats the answer to card 5 ("Wiped clean and flipped over") plus a joke, and tells nothing new from the passage.

rule.text: Every story card moves the baker forward through the passage. No recap cards.

findings.problem: "Not a crumb left" is presented as part of God's picture in 2 Kings 21:13, but the text only says wiping the bowl and turning it upside down. This adds to the text outside a joke.

rule.text: Don't stretch the text. Exaggerate only in his own jokes.

findings.problem: The right answer "idols" is an object of worship. The wrong answers "elders" and "nobles" are people nobody would be said to worship, so they are a different kind of thing and the right answer is obvious.

rule.text: All the answers are the same kind of thing, about the same length and the same tone. None are silly.

findings.problem: The card says "Then a plot forms against the king," which comes from 2 Kings 21:23, but it cites only 2 Kings 21:22. It should cite 2 Kings 21:22-23.

rule.text: Cite exactly what the card uses. Every story card cites the verses it tells, from the first verse it uses to the last, no wider and no narrower.

findings.problem: Many story cards have no voice at all and read as plain retelling, such as stop 1 cards 3, 7, 11 and 12 and stop 2 cards 8, 10, 15 and 18. The jokes that are there are mild, like the phone contract line on stop 2 card 12. There is room for real laughs on the non-somber moments, such as the twelve-year-old king, Amon's short reign, and the conspirators getting turned on.

rule.text: But he is FUNNY. Not mildly amusing. Laugh-out-loud funny, the kind a baker repeats to a friend. Because he talks naturally, the funny moments come up a lot: in his reactions, his comparisons, his disbelief and his self-deprecation. When a moment can hold a real laugh without muddying a fact, he goes for it. If a line reads like a nice dad being pleasant, push it further.
